name: Rainbow diet pills

lead: Rainbow diet pills were a regimen of several differently coloured pills taken at different times of day for weight loss. Typical mixes included amphetamine-type stimulants, thyroid hormone, diuretics, digitalis, laxatives and often a barbiturate to offset the stimulants.
The goal was a leaner body through appetite suppression and fluid loss. After deaths linked to diet pills in 1967 and 1968, a Senate investigation led to tighter restrictions in the United States.

paras: Historically the pills were prescribed in combination and taken at set times through the day. They were banned in the US in the late 1960s but reappeared in South America and Europe in the 1980s.

The combinations carried risks including palpitations, insomnia and cardiac effects, and deaths were linked to diet pills in the late 1960s. Regulators withdrew several of their component drug classes from the market over time.

angle.text: The regimen was meant to produce rapid weight loss. Its use has been associated with serious harms and it is documented here as history.

lead: Rainbow diet pills were multi-pill weight-loss regimens, taken throughout the day, that combined amphetamine-type stimulants, thyroid hormone, diuretics, digitalis, laxatives and often a barbiturate [1]. They were used to lose weight and achieve a slimmer appearance.

After deaths linked to diet pills in 1967 and 1968, a Senate investigation led to gradually tighter market restrictions, and the US banned rainbow pills in the late 1960s [1]. They resurfaced in South America and Europe in the 1980s [1].
Wikipedia's diet-pill article notes that thyroid hormone caused palpitations and insomnia and that many anti-obesity drugs have later been withdrawn over mental, cardiac and dependence concerns [1].
infobox: Stimulants, thyroid hormone, diuretics, digitalis, laxatives, barbiturate [1]

paras: The regimen consisted of several pills of different colours taken at different times [1]. Mixes typically combined amphetamine-type stimulants with thyroid hormone, diuretics, digitalis and laxatives, often with a barbiturate to counter stimulant side effects [1].

Deaths linked to diet pills in 1967 and 1968 led to a Senate investigation and gradually tighter restrictions [1]. The US banned the regimen in the late 1960s, and it reappeared in South America and Europe in the 1980s [1].

Thyroid hormone caused palpitations and insomnia [1]. Across 25 anti-obesity drugs withdrawn from 1964 to 2009, the most common reasons were mental disturbances, cardiac effects and abuse or dependence [1].
